items.stem: Which of the following statements about work is NOT correct?
items.markingKey: (b) "Work is a vector quantity." is false; the other three are true.
options: Work done by kinetic friction on a sliding body is negative.
Work is a vector quantity.
Work is the scalar product F·d.
The area under a force-displacement graph gives the work done.

items.stem: When can the work done by a force be negative? Give an example.
items.answer: When the angle between force and displacement is more than 90°, e.g. friction on a sliding block or gravity on a rising ball.
items.markingKey: Condition (1 mark); example (1 mark).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Work is a scalar quantity.
Reason (R): Work is the scalar product of force and displacement.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Meera pulls a trolley in a supermarket with a force of 10 N directed at 60° to the horizontal. How much work is done in moving it 10 m along the floor?
A force F = (8î + 7ĵ + 4k̂) N acts on a particle that is displaced by d = (6î − 2ĵ − 2k̂) m. Find the work done and the angle between F and d.
A force acting on a body along the x-axis is 4 N (constant) from x = 0 to x = 4 m and then changes linearly to 6 N at x = 12 m. Find the total work done by the force from x = 0 to x = 12 m.
items.markingKey: Area of rectangle = 4 × 4 = 16 J (1); trapezium = ½(4 + 6)(8) = 40 J (1); total 56 J (1).

items.stem: If F = (3î + 4ĵ) N and d = (4î − 3ĵ) m, the work done is
options: 7 J
0 J

items.stem: A 10 kg block slides 4 m down a rough plane inclined at 60° (μₖ = 0.1). Find the work done on it by (i) gravity, (ii) friction and (iii) the normal force, and the net work. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.markingKey: (i) W_g = mgL sin θ = 339 J (1). (ii) W_f = −μmg cos θ · L = −19.6 J (1). (iii) N ⊥ displacement ⇒ 0; net = 320 J (1).

items.stem: Sneha pulls a trolley in a supermarket with a force of 50 N directed at 30° to the horizontal. How much work is done in moving it 8 m along the floor?
items.markingKey: W = Fd cos θ = 50 × 8 × cos 30° = 346 J.

items.stem: How much work is needed to stretch a spring of spring constant 500 N m⁻¹ from an extension of 2 cm to 8 cm?
Why is the work done by the centripetal force on a body moving in a circle zero?
items.answer: The centripetal force is always perpendicular to the velocity (displacement).

items.stem: A 10 kg block slides 2 m down a rough plane inclined at 45° (μₖ = 0.2). Find the work done on it by (i) gravity, (ii) friction and (iii) the normal force, and the net work. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.markingKey: (i) W_g = mgL sin θ = 139 J (1). (ii) W_f = −μmg cos θ · L = −27.7 J (1). (iii) N ⊥ displacement ⇒ 0; net = 111 J (1).

items.stem: Which of the following statements about work is correct?
items.answer: Work done by kinetic friction on a sliding body is negative.
items.markingKey: (c) Correct: "Work done by kinetic friction on a sliding body is negative." The other three are false.
options: Work done by a force is always positive.
Work done by the centripetal force in uniform circular motion is positive.
Work done by kinetic friction on a sliding body is negative.
A coolie carrying a load on his head and walking on a level road does positive work against gravity.

items.stem: Explain why the work done by a variable force is found from the area under the force-displacement graph.
items.answer: Splitting the displacement into small steps, W = ΣF Δx, which becomes ∫F dx: the area under the graph.
items.markingKey: Small-step sum (1 mark); integral = area (1 mark).

items.stem: Which of the following statements about kinetic energy and the work-energy theorem is correct?
items.answer: The work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: (a) Correct: "The work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy." The other three are false.
options: The work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy.
Doubling the speed of a body doubles its kinetic energy.
The potential energy of a spring is ½kx regardless of the sign of x.
For the same momentum, a heavier body has more kinetic energy.

items.stem: Why is the potential energy of a spring the same whether it is stretched or compressed by x?
items.answer: V = ½kx² depends on x², which is the same for +x and −x.
items.markingKey: Formula (1 mark); x² argument (1 mark).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The work done by the net force on a body moving with constant speed in a circle is zero.
Reason (R): Its kinetic energy does not change.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) By the work-energy theorem, W = ΔK = 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Find the kinetic energy of a 60 kg sprinter moving at 8 m s⁻¹.
A car of mass 1500 kg moving at 90 km h⁻¹ is brought to rest by a constant braking force of 4000 N. Use the work-energy theorem to find the stopping distance.

A raindrop of mass 1.5 g falls from a height of 0.8 km and hits the ground with a speed of 25 m s⁻¹. Find (i) the work done by gravity and (ii) the work done by the unknown resistive force of air. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
A block of mass 0.5 kg moving at 4 m s⁻¹ on a smooth floor hits a spring (k = 800 N m⁻¹) fixed at its far end. Find the maximum compression of the spring.

To simulate car accidents, a car of mass 1000 kg moving at 36 km h⁻¹ on a horizontal road collides with a horizontally mounted spring of constant 5000 N m⁻¹. Taking the coefficient of kinetic friction as 0.5, find the maximum compression of the spring. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.markingKey: ½mv² = ½kx² + μmgx (2): ½ × 1000 × 10² = 2500x² + 4900x (1); solve the quadratic, take the positive root: x = 3.60 m (2). (Without friction x would be 4.47 m.)

items.stem: Two bodies of masses 5 kg and 1 kg have equal linear momenta. Find the ratio of their kinetic energies K₁ : K₂.
items.markingKey: K = p²/2m, so K₁/K₂ = m₂/m₁ = 1/5 = 0.200.

items.stem: Show that the potential energy stored in a spring stretched by x is ½kx².
items.markingKey: Spring force −kx (1); work by applied force ∫₀ˣ kx dx (2) = ½kx² stored as PE (2).

items.stem: Find the kinetic energy of a 0.16 kg cricket ball moving at 35 m s⁻¹.
A light body and a heavy body have the same momentum. Which has more kinetic energy? Explain.
items.markingKey: K = p²/2m; for the same p, K ∝ 1/m (2 marks).

items.stem: Which of the following statements about kinetic energy and the work-energy theorem is correct?
items.answer: For the same momentum, a lighter body has more kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: (a) Correct: "For the same momentum, a lighter body has more kinetic energy." The other three are false.
options: For the same momentum, a lighter body has more kinetic energy.
The work done by the net force equals the change in potential energy.
The potential energy of a spring is ½kx regardless of the sign of x.
For the same momentum, a heavier body has more kinetic energy.

items.stem: Two bodies of masses 5 kg and 10 kg have equal linear momenta. Find the ratio of their kinetic energies K₁ : K₂.
items.markingKey: K = p²/2m, so K₁/K₂ = m₂/m₁ = 10/5 = 2.00.

items.stem: A raindrop falls at terminal velocity. Is the work-energy theorem violated since gravity does work but the KE stays the same?
items.answer: No: air resistance does equal negative work, so the net work and the change in KE are both zero.
items.markingKey: Net work = 0 (1 mark); ΔK = 0 (1 mark).

items.stem: A block of mass 1 kg moving at 3 m s⁻¹ on a smooth floor hits a spring (k = 1000 N m⁻¹) fixed at its far end. Find the maximum compression of the spring.
Which of the following statements about mechanical energy and power is NOT correct?
items.answer: Mechanical energy is conserved even when friction acts.
items.markingKey: (d) "Mechanical energy is conserved even when friction acts." is false; the other three are true.
options: Mechanical energy is conserved when only conservative forces do work.
Work done by a conservative force around a closed path is zero.
Instantaneous power P = F·v.
Mechanical energy is conserved even when friction acts.

items.stem: What is a conservative force? Give one example of a conservative and one of a non-conservative force.
items.answer: A force whose work depends only on the end points (zero around a closed path), e.g. gravity; friction is non-conservative.
items.markingKey: Definition (1 mark); examples (1 mark).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): For a vehicle moving at constant velocity on a rough road the engine power is F·v.
Reason (R): Instantaneous power is the dot product of force and velocity.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A pump on the ground floor of a building in Jaipur can pump up water to fill a tank of volume 2000 L on the roof 25 m high in 5 min. If the efficiency of the pump is 75%, how much electric power does it consume? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²; 1 L of water = 1 kg)
items.markingKey: Useful power = mgh/t = 2000 × 9.8 × 25/(5 × 60) = 1630 W; input = useful/efficiency = 2180 W.

items.stem: A pendulum bob on a string 2 m long is pulled aside until the string makes 45° with the vertical, and released. Find its speed at the lowest point. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.markingKey: Height fall h = L(1 − cos θ) = 0.5858 m; v = √(2gh) = 3.39 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: An elevator with a maximum load of 1800 kg (elevator + passengers) moves up with a constant speed of 3 m s⁻¹. The frictional force opposing the motion is 2000 N. Find the minimum power delivered by the motor in watt and in horsepower. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²; 1 hp = 746 W)
Why is the kilowatt-hour a unit of energy and not of power?
items.answer: It is power (kW) multiplied by time (h); 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
items.markingKey: Power × time = energy (1 mark); conversion (1 mark).

items.stem: A 750 W water pump is used for 6 hours every day. How many units (kWh) of electricity does it consume in 30 days, and what is the cost at ₹5 per unit?
A bob of mass m tied to a string of length 1 m is to complete a vertical circle. Find the minimum speeds at the lowest and highest points. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.answer: Lowest 7.00 m s⁻¹; highest 3.13 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: At the top, T ≥ 0 ⇒ mv²/L ≥ mg ⇒ v_top = √(gL) = 3.13 m s⁻¹ (1.5). Energy: ½mv_b² = ½mv_t² + 2mgL ⇒ v_b = √(5gL) = 7.00 m s⁻¹ (1.5).

items.stem:
At a small hydroelectric plant in Himachal Pradesh, water falls through a height of 50 m and 400 kg of water passes through the turbine every second. Tanvi learns that the plant converts 80% of the water's potential energy into electrical energy. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
(i) Find the potential energy lost by the water per second. (ii) Find the electrical power output. (iii) Find the speed of the water just before reaching the turbine (no losses). (iv) Name one form into which the remaining energy is converted.
items.answer: (i) 1.96 × 10⁵ J (ii) 157 kW (iii) 31.3 m s⁻¹ (iv) heat/sound (internal energy)
items.markingKey: (i) mgh per second = 1.96 × 10⁵ J (1). (ii) 80% of it = 1.57 × 10⁵ W (1). (iii) √(2gh) (1). (iv) heat, sound or friction losses (1).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The kilowatt-hour is a unit of power.
Reason (R): 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false (it is a unit of energy); R is true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about mechanical energy and power is correct?
items.answer: Work done by a conservative force around a closed path is zero.
items.markingKey: (c) Correct: "Work done by a conservative force around a closed path is zero." The other three are false.
options: Power is a vector quantity.
Mechanical energy is conserved even when friction acts.
Work done by a conservative force around a closed path is zero.
The kilowatt-hour is a unit of power.

items.stem: A child slides from rest down a frictionless slide in a park. The top is 7.5 m above the bottom. Find the child's speed at the bottom. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.markingKey: mgh = ½mv² ⇒ v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 7.5) = 12.1 m s⁻¹ (independent of the shape of the slide).

items.stem: A 60 W fan is used for 3 hours every day. How many units (kWh) of electricity does it consume in 30 days, and what is the cost at ₹5 per unit?
Which of the following statements about collisions is NOT correct?
items.answer: In a completely inelastic collision no kinetic energy is lost.
items.markingKey: (d) "In a completely inelastic collision no kinetic energy is lost." is false; the other three are true.
options: Linear momentum is conserved in all collisions if no external force acts.
In a completely inelastic collision, the loss of kinetic energy is maximum.
In an elastic head-on collision of equal masses (one at rest), the velocities are exchanged.
In a completely inelastic collision no kinetic energy is lost.

items.stem: In nuclear reactors, why is a moderator with light nuclei (like heavy water) used to slow down neutrons?
items.answer: In an elastic collision a neutron loses most energy when the target mass is close to its own.
items.markingKey: Energy transfer 4m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)² is maximum for m₁ = m₂ (2 marks).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): In an elastic collision between equal masses, one at rest, the moving body stops.
Reason (R): v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂).
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) With m₁ = m₂, v₁ = 0; R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A trolley of mass 2 kg moving at 10 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary trolley of mass 5 kg and they move off together. Find their common velocity and the loss in kinetic energy.
A ball of mass 2 kg moving at 3 m s⁻¹ makes a head-on elastic collision with a ball of mass 3 kg at rest. Find their velocities after the collision.
items.answer: v₁ = −0.600 m s⁻¹, v₂ = 2.40 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂) = −0.600 m s⁻¹ (rebounds); v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂) = 2.40 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A bullet of mass 10 g moving horizontally at 400 m s⁻¹ gets embedded in a wooden block of mass 5 kg hanging from long strings. To what height does the block rise? What fraction of the bullet's KE is lost? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.markingKey: Momentum: V = mv/(m + M) = 0.798 m s⁻¹ (1); energy after collision: h = V²/2g = 0.0325 m (1); fraction lost = M/(m + M) = 99.8% (1).

items.stem: A neutron (mass 1 u) makes a head-on elastic collision with a hydrogen nucleus (mass 1 u) at rest. What fraction of its kinetic energy is transferred to the nucleus?
items.markingKey: Fraction = 4m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)² = 4 × 1/4 = 1.00.

items.stem: At a crossing, a car of mass 1000 kg moving east at 12 m s⁻¹ collides with a car of mass 1500 kg moving north at 16 m s⁻¹. They lock together. Find their velocity just after the collision.
items.answer: 10.7 m s⁻¹ at 63.4° north of east

items.stem: Why is momentum conserved in a collision even though large forces act?
items.answer: The forces are internal: equal and opposite on the two bodies, so the total momentum does not change.
items.markingKey: Third law pairs (1 mark); no external impulse (1 mark).

items.stem: Which type of collision is described: both total linear momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved?
items.markingKey: (c) elastic collision: both total linear momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved.
options: inelastic collision
head-on (one-dimensional) collision
elastic collision
completely inelastic collision

items.stem: Show that in a completely inelastic collision of m₁ (speed u₁) with m₂ at rest, the loss of kinetic energy is ½ m₁m₂u₁²/(m₁ + m₂).
items.markingKey: v = m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂) (2); ΔK = ½m₁u₁² − ½(m₁ + m₂)v² (2); simplify (1).

items.stem: A ball dropped from a height of 20 m loses 10% of its kinetic energy at every bounce on the floor. How high does it rise after the 2nd bounce? What is the total kinetic energy fraction lost by then?
items.markingKey: After each bounce, height ∝ KE just after: h_k = h(1 − 0.1)ᵏ (2); h_2 = 20 × 0.9^2 = 16.2 m (2); lost fraction 1 − 0.9^2 (1).

items.stem: A neutron (mass 1 u) makes a head-on elastic collision with a carbon nucleus (mass 12 u) at rest. What fraction of its kinetic energy is transferred to the nucleus?
items.markingKey: Fraction = 4m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)² = 4 × 12/169 = 0.284.

items.stem: Show that in a one-dimensional elastic collision of two equal masses, one initially at rest, the velocities are exchanged.
items.answer: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂) = 0 and v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂) = u.
items.markingKey: Formulae (1 mark); substitution m₁ = m₂ (1 mark).

items.stem: A bullet of mass 20 g moving horizontally at 300 m s⁻¹ gets embedded in a wooden block of mass 4 kg hanging from long strings. To what height does the block rise? What fraction of the bullet's KE is lost? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.markingKey: Momentum: V = mv/(m + M) = 1.49 m s⁻¹ (1); energy after collision: h = V²/2g = 0.114 m (1); fraction lost = M/(m + M) = 99.5% (1).

items.stem:
Nandini is playing carrom-style billiards. A striker of mass 200 g moving at 1.5 m s⁻¹ hits an identical stationary ball head-on.
(i) If the collision is elastic, find the velocities after collision. (ii) If instead they stick together, find the common velocity. (iii) Find the KE lost in case (ii). (iv) In which case is momentum conserved?
items.answer: (i) striker 0, ball 1.5 m s⁻¹ (ii) 0.75 m s⁻¹ (iii) 0.113 J (iv) both
items.markingKey: (i) equal masses exchange velocities (1). (ii) v = u/2 (1). (iii) ½mu² − ½(2m)(u/2)² = ¼mu² = 0.113 J (1). (iv) both (1).

items.stem: Derive the work-energy theorem for a variable force using calculus.
items.markingKey: dK/dt = mv dv/dt = Fv (2); dK = F dx (1); integrate from x_i to x_f (2).

items.stem: A bob is released from a horizontal position. Explain, using energy, why its speed is greatest at the lowest point.
items.answer: Potential energy is least there, so (with mechanical energy conserved) kinetic energy is greatest.
items.markingKey: K + U constant (1 mark); U minimum at bottom (1 mark).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A person standing still holding a heavy box does no work on the box.
Reason (R): The box has no displacement.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) W = F·d = 0 because d = 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A trolley of mass 5 kg moving at 3 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary trolley of mass 4 kg and they move off together. Find their common velocity and the loss in kinetic energy.

Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

items.stem: To simulate car accidents, a car of mass 1200 kg moving at 18 km h⁻¹ on a horizontal road collides with a horizontally mounted spring of constant 6250 N m⁻¹. Taking the coefficient of kinetic friction as 0.3, find the maximum compression of the spring. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.markingKey: ½mv² = ½kx² + μmgx (2): ½ × 1200 × 5² = 3125x² + 3528x (1); solve the quadratic, take the positive root: x = 1.70 m (2). (Without friction x would be 2.19 m.)

items.stem: A pump on the ground floor of a building in Dehradun can pump up water to fill a tank of volume 1500 L on the roof 30 m high in 5 min. If the efficiency of the pump is 80%, how much electric power does it consume? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²; 1 L of water = 1 kg)
items.markingKey: Useful power = mgh/t = 1500 × 9.8 × 30/(5 × 60) = 1470 W; input = useful/efficiency = 1840 W.

items.answer: 10.7 m s⁻¹ at 38.7° north of east

items.markingKey: W = Fd cos θ = 40 × 12 × cos 60° = 240 J.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about collisions is correct?
items.answer: In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy after equals the total before.
items.markingKey: (c) Correct: "In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy after equals the total before." The other three are false.

items.markingKey: v² − u² = 2as (1); multiply by m/2: ½mv² − ½mu² = mas = Fs (2); Fs = W, so W = ΔK (2).

items.stem: A ball dropped from a height does not bounce back to the same height. Is energy conserved? Explain.
items.answer: Total energy is conserved, but some mechanical energy changes into heat, sound and deformation.
items.markingKey: Total vs mechanical energy (1 mark); forms (1 mark).

items.stem: A trolley of mass 5 kg moving at 2 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary trolley of mass 1 kg and they move off together. Find their common velocity and the loss in kinetic energy.

Assertion (A): In an oblique elastic collision of equal masses with one at rest, they move off at right angles.
Reason (R): Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) u² = v₁² + v₂² with u = v₁ + v₂ forces v₁ ⊥ v₂; R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: To simulate car accidents, a car of mass 1000 kg moving at 18 km h⁻¹ on a horizontal road collides with a horizontally mounted spring of constant 10000 N m⁻¹. Taking the coefficient of kinetic friction as 0.5, find the maximum compression of the spring. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
items.markingKey: ½mv² = ½kx² + μmgx (2): ½ × 1000 × 5² = 5000x² + 4900x (1); solve the quadratic, take the positive root: x = 1.17 m (2). (Without friction x would be 1.58 m.)

items.stem: A pump on the ground floor of a building in Patna can pump up water to fill a tank of volume 1000 L on the roof 30 m high in 30 min. If the efficiency of the pump is 60%, how much electric power does it consume? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²; 1 L of water = 1 kg)
items.markingKey: Useful power = mgh/t = 1000 × 9.8 × 30/(30 × 60) = 163 W; input = useful/efficiency = 272 W.

items.stem: Farhan pulls a trolley in a supermarket with a force of 10 N directed at 37° to the horizontal. How much work is done in moving it 5 m along the floor?
items.markingKey: W = Fd cos θ = 10 × 5 × cos 37° = 39.9 J.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about collisions is NOT correct?
items.answer: In a completely inelastic collision no kinetic energy is lost.
items.markingKey: (c) "In a completely inelastic collision no kinetic energy is lost." is false; the other three are true.
options: Linear momentum is conserved in all collisions if no external force acts.
In a completely inelastic collision, the loss of kinetic energy is maximum.
In a completely inelastic collision no kinetic energy is lost.
In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy after equals the total before.

items.stem: A raindrop of mass 1.5 g falls from a height of 1 km and hits the ground with a speed of 10 m s⁻¹. Find (i) the work done by gravity and (ii) the work done by the unknown resistive force of air. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
A force acting on a body along the x-axis is 5 N (constant) from x = 0 to x = 5 m and then changes linearly to 6 N at x = 10 m. Find the total work done by the force from x = 0 to x = 10 m.
items.markingKey: Area of rectangle = 5 × 5 = 25 J (1); trapezium = ½(5 + 6)(5) = 27.5 J (1); total 52.5 J (1).

items.markingKey: (a) "Friction is a conservative force." is false; the other three are true.

The SI unit of power is the watt (J s⁻¹).
